RQ1 — Does the corpus follow Zipf?: The rank-frequency curves have a high-frequency head and a long rare-term tail, with an approximately linear middle on log-log axes. For condition B, the full-vocabulary fit has R²=0.9687 and log10 RMSE=0.0975. The exponent differs from the idealized value 1; the corpus is Zipf-like rather than an exact 1/r distribution. Among predefined regions with nonconstant frequencies, Head (0–10%) has the smallest log-space RMSE (0.0411, R²=0.9900). The complete regional table and residuals show where the approximation changes. R² alone is insufficient: it measures a descriptive OLS fit after a logarithmic transformation. Ranked observations are dependent, many tail frequencies are tied, and no competing distribution or formal power-law goodness-of-fit test is evaluated. Constant tails have undefined R², not proof of an exact law.
RQ2 — What is the empirical exponent?: With log10(CF)=a+m*log10(rank), k=-m. Full-vocabulary estimates are A: 1.0915, B: 1.2508, C: 1.2095, D: 1.2663. Condition B has slope -1.2508, intercept 5.2149, and k=1.2508. The estimate depends on preprocessing and the fitted rank range. The 1/r reference is anchored to the most frequent term; it is not the fitted regression line.
RQ3 — How does preprocessing affect the: A contains 245,416 tokens and 28,792 distinct terms. Boundary punctuation normalization reduces vocabulary to 19,231 in B, while retaining internal punctuation in biomedical identifiers such as GLP-1. Stopword removal reduces tokens from 243,843 to 177,052; vocabulary becomes 19,115. Porter then reduces vocabulary to 15,569 (18.55% below C), with 177,052 retained tokens. Punctuation merges surface variants, stopwords reshape the head, and stemming combines morphological forms throughout the curve. Neither a smaller vocabulary nor an exponent closer to one proves better retrieval. Inspect the Top 50 tables and merged forms for specific examples.
RQ4 — What is the relationship between C: CF counts occurrences; DF counts distinct documents. In condition B, 'and' occurs 10,988 times across 997 abstracts, with IDF=0.0030. In contrast, 'cdr' has CF=15, DF=1 and CF/DF=15.00: repetition is concentrated rather than widespread. A paper can repeat a specialized abbreviation many times, raising CF while contributing only one to DF. DF/N directly describes document coverage. Both measures matter: CF captures repetition and processing volume; DF determines postings-list coverage and collection-level discrimination. IDF=ln(N/DF) is smaller for terms occurring in many documents. CF alone cannot determine IDF, because equal CF can have different DF.
RQ5 — Why does Zipf matter to IR?:
Zipf's law matters because an information retrieval system processes a highly uneven vocabulary. In this collection, condition B contains 19,231 distinct terms and 243,843 occurrences. A small head contributes many occurrences, while numerous rare forms occupy the tail. This structure connects language statistics to indexing cost and term weighting. It is an empirical design guide rather than a rule that every biomedical collection must satisfy exactly.

Stopword removal changes the workload substantially: condition C retains 177,052 tokens, compared with 243,843 in B. Common grammatical words often occur in most documents, so their presence provides little evidence that one paper is more relevant than another. Removing them can shorten query processing and positional data. However, frequent words are not automatically useless: phrases, negation, and biomedical concepts may depend on them. The experiment demonstrates changed counts, not an improvement in retrieval effectiveness. Phrase search should therefore preserve the original text and use an explicitly documented matching policy.

For an inverted index, each unique term needs a dictionary entry and a postings list. High-DF terms have long document lists; high-CF terms may also have many stored positions. The long tail creates many short lists and dictionary entries, even when each term has few occurrences. Porter reduces vocabulary from 19,115 to 15,569 between C and D, suggesting a smaller dictionary, but merged lists may become longer. Actual storage also depends on document-ID gaps, position encoding and implementation overhead. Gap-based integer compression and compact dictionaries are relevant design options; this study does not claim measured compression savings.

TF-IDF separates within-document repetition from collection-wide prevalence. Raw TF can reward a term repeated in a document, while IDF=ln(N/DF) discounts terms shared by many documents. A term found in every document has IDF zero under this formula. High CF alone does not imply low IDF: a specialized term can be repeated heavily in only a few abstracts. Comparing CF and DF reveals this distinction. Zipf's head helps explain why frequency alone is an inadequate ranking signal, but DF must be measured independently. Helix keeps BM25 ranking separate from this textbook-IDF analysis. Ultimately, frequency statistics justify concrete experiments on index size, query latency and relevance judgments; they cannot replace those evaluations.
Final challenge — Why is an approximate: The four conditions produce different exponents (A: 1.0915, B: 1.2508, C: 1.2095, D: 1.2663), yet all show strongly uneven term frequencies. That robust qualitative structure is useful even though no single exact law explains every rank. It motivates separate treatment of very common terms, compact storage for a large rare-term vocabulary, and weighting based on document coverage. These are engineering hypotheses supported by observed counts, not universal guarantees. This study measures vocabulary reduction and frequency structure; it does not measure compressed index bytes or retrieval relevance. A subsequent evaluation should compare latency, actual storage, and judged search quality before claiming an improvement. The useful lesson is to let the empirical curve guide design, then validate the design against the system's retrieval objective.
